lessonTitle: Vaccine Types and Mechanisms: Live, Inactivated, Subunit, Conjugate and mRNA

blocks.text: Plain pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide vaccine works reasonably well in a healthy adult yet fails in a one-year-old, who has almost no response to it and no memory afterwards. Chemically attaching the same sugar to a protein changes the outcome completely. Understanding why explains much of modern vaccine design, from adjuvants to mRNA.

blocks.markdown: A vaccine presents an immune system with **antigen** in a safe form so that it generates **memory B and T cells** and protective antibody before a real infection. Vaccine platforms differ in how the antigen is delivered, which determines how strong, how durable and how safe the response is, and who can receive it.

blocks.caption: Vaccine platforms
rows: Weakened organism that replicates in the host without causing significant disease
MMR, varicella, BCG, yellow fever, oral rotavirus, oral polio (Sabin)
Whole organism killed by heat or chemicals; cannot replicate
Purified protein or particle containing selected antigens
Hepatitis B surface antigen, HPV virus-like particle, acellular pertussis
Polysaccharide covalently linked to a carrier protein
Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcal conjugate, meningococcal conjugate
Lipid nanoparticle carrying mRNA that encodes an antigen

blocks.markdown: **Live attenuated versus inactivated.** A live vaccine **replicates** in the vaccinee and mimics natural infection: it exposes antigen in infected cells so it stimulates both **antibody** and **cytotoxic T-cell** responses (endogenous antigen is presented on MHC class I), often with strong, **long-lasting immunity after one or two doses**, and in some cases mucosal immunity. Disadvantages: the weakened organism can cause **disease in immunosuppressed** people, rarely reverts to virulence (for example vaccine-derived poliovirus from the oral polio vaccine), and live vaccines generally need a strict cold chain. Inactivated vaccines **cannot replicate**, so they are safer in immunosuppressed people and more stable, but are usually **less immunogenic**, mainly produce antibody (exogenous antigen is presented on MHC class II), and typically require **multiple doses and boosters** and often an adjuvant.

blocks.caption: Live attenuated compared with inactivated vaccines
rows: High; antibody and cell-mediated; often long-lasting
Generally safe, though response may be reduced

blocks.title: Choosing a platform
blocks.prompt: A patient is about to begin high-dose immunosuppressive treatment after a transplant and needs protection against influenza. Should a live or an inactivated vaccine be chosen, and why?

steps.text: Live attenuated vaccines replicate; in an immunosuppressed person the weakened organism might cause disease.
Inactivated vaccines cannot replicate and so are safe, although the response may be weaker and a booster or higher-antigen dose may be used.

blocks.answer: An inactivated vaccine, because it cannot replicate and is safe in profound immunosuppression.

blocks.markdown: **Adjuvants.** An adjuvant is a substance added to a vaccine to **enhance the immune response** to a poorly immunogenic antigen. **Aluminium salts** (alum) are the most widely used: they form a depot, help antigen uptake by antigen-presenting cells and activate innate immune pathways (including the inflammasome), increasing antibody production. Newer adjuvants include Toll-like receptor agonists. Adjuvants allow smaller antigen doses and improve responses in older people. They are most important for **subunit, toxoid and inactivated** vaccines, whose pure antigens give little danger signal; live vaccines contain their own innate immune stimuli.

**Conjugation.** Bacterial capsular polysaccharides are **T-cell-independent antigens**: they cross-link B-cell receptors without help from T cells, giving short-lived IgM-dominant responses, little class switching and **no immunological memory**, and infants under about two years respond poorly. In a **conjugate vaccine**, the polysaccharide is covalently linked to a **carrier protein** (for example tetanus toxoid). B cells recognising the sugar internalise the whole conjugate and present **carrier peptides on MHC class II** to T-helper cells. This provides T-cell help, so the response becomes **T-dependent**, with class switching to IgG, affinity maturation, **memory** and responses in infants. Conjugate vaccines also reduce nasopharyngeal carriage and so contribute to herd immunity.

**How an mRNA vaccine works.** The vaccine contains messenger RNA encoding an antigen (for example a viral spike protein), enclosed in **lipid nanoparticles** that protect the RNA and carry it into host cells after intramuscular injection. Once in the cytoplasm, the cell's **ribosomes translate** the mRNA into the antigen protein, so the antigen is made by the host cell and **presented on MHC class I and class II**, activating CD8 and CD4 T cells, and is also released or displayed so that B cells make neutralising antibody. The mRNA does not enter the nucleus or integrate into the genome, and it is **degraded within days**. Chemical modification of nucleosides reduces unwanted innate sensing, while the lipid nanoparticle provides some adjuvant activity.

blocks.title: Explaining an mRNA vaccine response
blocks.prompt: Trace the steps from injection of an mRNA vaccine to protective antibody.

steps.text: Lipid nanoparticles deliver mRNA into cells at the injection site and draining lymph nodes.
Ribosomes translate the mRNA into the antigen protein; the antigen is processed and presented on MHC class I and II and is also exposed to B cells.
T-helper cells help B cells in germinal centres, giving class-switched, high-affinity antibody and memory cells; CD8 T cells are also primed.
The mRNA is degraded and the antigen production is transient.

blocks.answer: Delivery by lipid nanoparticle, translation into antigen, T and B cell activation, memory; no genome integration.

blocks.caption: Vaccine efficacy: ARU is attack rate in the unvaccinated; ARV is attack rate in the vaccinated

blocks.title: Matching platform to need
blocks.text: Live vaccines give the strongest, longest immunity but need healthy immune systems; inactivated, subunit and conjugate vaccines are safer but need adjuvants, boosters or carrier proteins; mRNA vaccines use the host cell to make the antigen.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Plain polysaccharide vaccines do not give memory or reliable infant protection; conjugation solves this. mRNA vaccines do not alter DNA. Adjuvants are not preservatives.

points: Live attenuated vaccines are highly immunogenic but unsuitable in severe immunosuppression; inactivated vaccines are safer but weaker and need boosters.

Adjuvants such as aluminium salts enhance responses to poorly immunogenic antigens; conjugation to a carrier protein converts a T-independent polysaccharide response into a T-dependent one with memory.
mRNA vaccines deliver mRNA in lipid nanoparticles; host ribosomes make the antigen, which activates T and B cells.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares live attenuated and inactivated vaccines?

options.text: Live attenuated vaccines are usually more immunogenic but are unsuitable in severe immunosuppression
Inactivated vaccines are more immunogenic and need only one dose
Live vaccines cannot replicate in the host
Inactivated vaccines can revert to virulence

questions.correctOptionText: Live attenuated vaccines are usually more immunogenic but are unsuitable in severe immunosuppression

distractorRationale.b: Inactivated vaccines are usually less immunogenic and need boosters.

questions.explanation: Replication of a live vaccine mimics natural infection and gives strong immunity, but the replicating organism is a risk where immunity is weak. Inactivated vaccines trade potency for safety.

questions.stem: Which vaccine is an example of a live attenuated vaccine?

options.text: Measles-mumps-rubella vaccine
Tetanus toxoid
Hepatitis B recombinant surface antigen vaccine
Inactivated poliovirus vaccine

distractorRationale.c: Hepatitis B vaccine is a subunit vaccine.

questions.explanation: MMR contains weakened viruses that replicate in the vaccinee. The other options are non-replicating.

questions.stem: Why does conjugating a capsular polysaccharide to a carrier protein improve the response in infants?

options.text: It recruits T-helper cell help, converting a T-independent response into a T-dependent one with class switching and memory
It makes the sugar replicate in the host
It kills the bacterium
It removes the need for B cells

questions.correctOptionText: It recruits T-helper cell help, converting a T-independent response into a T-dependent one with class switching and memory

distractorRationale.c: Vaccines do not kill the bacterium directly.

questions.explanation: B cells present peptides from the carrier protein on MHC class II to T-helper cells, which provide help. This produces IgG, affinity maturation and memory, which the polysaccharide alone cannot.

questions.stem: What is the main role of an aluminium salt adjuvant in an inactivated vaccine?

options.text: To enhance the immune response to the antigen, partly by forming a depot and activating innate immunity
To preserve the vaccine against bacterial contamination
To make the antigen replicate
To prevent any local reaction

questions.correctOptionText: To enhance the immune response to the antigen, partly by forming a depot and activating innate immunity
questions.explanation: Pure antigens give little danger signal, so an adjuvant boosts antigen uptake and innate activation. This yields higher and longer-lasting antibody levels.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes how an mRNA vaccine induces an immune response?

options.text: Lipid nanoparticles deliver mRNA into cells, host ribosomes translate it into antigen, and the antigen is presented to T cells and recognised by B cells
The mRNA integrates into host DNA, which then makes antigen permanently
The mRNA replicates indefinitely in the nucleus
The mRNA is itself the antigen recognised by antibody

questions.correctOptionText: Lipid nanoparticles deliver mRNA into cells, host ribosomes translate it into antigen, and the antigen is presented to T cells and recognised by B cells

distractorRationale.b: mRNA does not integrate into the genome.
distractorRationale.c: It does not enter or replicate in the nucleus and is degraded within days.
distractorRationale.d: The encoded protein is the antigen.

questions.explanation: The host cell becomes the factory for the antigen, so it is presented on MHC molecules and activates T and B cells. The mRNA is short-lived.

questions.stem: In a trial, 40 of 2 000 unvaccinated participants and 4 of 2 000 vaccinated participants develop the disease during follow-up. Using VE = (ARU - ARV) / ARU x 100, calculate the vaccine efficacy as a percentage.
An antibody titre is 1:20 before vaccination and 1:1 280 four weeks after the second dose. Calculate the fold rise in titre.
questions.explanation: Fold rise = 1280 / 20 = 64, which is 2^6, or six doublings. Fold rise in titre is a standard measure of immunogenicity, with a four-fold rise commonly used to define seroconversion in paired samples.

questions.stem: Compare live attenuated and inactivated vaccines in terms of immunogenicity, type of immune response, safety and dosing.
markingGuide: Live vaccine replicates and mimics natural infection
Stronger and longer-lasting immunity, antibody and cell-mediated (MHC class I presentation), often fewer doses
Risks: disease in immunosuppressed people, rare reversion, cold chain
Inactivated cannot replicate, safer in immunosuppression and stable
Less immunogenic, mainly antibody, needs adjuvants and boosters
questions.explanation: Replication gives potency but carries risk; non-replicating vaccines are safer but weaker. The choice depends on the patient and the pathogen.

questions.stem: Explain why plain capsular polysaccharide vaccines are poorly immunogenic in infants, and how conjugation to a carrier protein and the use of adjuvants improve vaccine responses.
markingGuide: Polysaccharides are T-independent antigens: limited class switching, no memory, poor infant response
Conjugation links polysaccharide to carrier protein; B cell presents carrier peptide on MHC II to T-helper cells
T-cell help gives IgG, affinity maturation and memory, including in infants
Adjuvants (such as aluminium salts) enhance innate activation and antigen uptake for poorly immunogenic antigens
Conjugate vaccines also reduce carriage and aid herd immunity
questions.explanation: T-cell help is the key difference between a polysaccharide and a conjugate. Adjuvants address a separate problem: weak innate stimulation by purified antigens.

questions.stem: Describe how an mRNA vaccine induces an immune response and why it does not alter the recipient's DNA.
markingGuide: mRNA encoding antigen is delivered in lipid nanoparticles to cells after injection
Host ribosomes in the cytoplasm translate it to antigen
Antigen presented on MHC class I and II activates CD8 and CD4 T cells; B cells make antibody with T-cell help and memory
Lipid nanoparticle and modified nucleosides influence innate sensing and adjuvant activity
mRNA stays in the cytoplasm, is not reverse-transcribed or integrated and is degraded within days
questions.explanation: The host cell makes the antigen, so both antibody and T-cell responses can occur. mRNA is transient and does not enter the nucleus.
